newsitem.title: UK: Political risk is not dead, but it may move house. [CORRECTED 11:58 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Political risk is not dead, but it may move house. [CORRECTED 11:58 GMT]

text.p: Change in leadership of the world's major political and economic powers was, in the past, a potentially catastrophic event for financial markets.
Now, as Russian President Boris Yeltsin battles with serious heart problems and U.S. President Bill Clinton fights for re-election, markets are playing it much cooler.
But analysts warned political risk is not dead, and could yet rear up again in the most unlikely places -- the apparently rock steady core of Europe.
"The key thing is whether the disappearance of Clinton and Yeltsin would change the world," said Stephen Bell, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
"And the truth is -- not very much."
In the 1980s, the lingering cold war and worldwide economic recession provided a volatile mix for the markets.
But with the Soviet empire now fragmented and capitalist economic orthodoxy taking root across the world, financial markets have become increasingly inured to political shocks.
Analysts noted two 1990 crises -- the coup which briefly ousted then Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev (Corrects from Russian President Boris Yeltsin) and the Gulf War.
In both cases, major market reactions were later judged to be overreactions and reversed.
Now, U.S. bombing of Iraq or calls for Yeltsin to resign give only a faint boost to the dollar or gold, usually safe-haven investments in times of perceived crisis.
"Political risk is relevant, but the old days when you'd see five or even 10 big figures movement on dollar/mark. Those days are over," said Bell.
Analysts say two main factors have reduced markets' sensitivity to political turmoil.

"Since the fall of the Soviet Union, markets have been crying wolf about Russia, so the impact of every twist and turn in Russian politics is getting smaller," said Stuart Thomson, chief international economist at Nikko in London.

"(Russia) is a very small part of western trade, the economy is not going to collapse to the extent that you would see thousands of refugees flood over the borders. So, all those previous scare stories are being put into a proper perspective."
Convergence in major industrialised nations toward low inflation, sustained growth and some unemployment has also meant few fundamental economic moves from government changes.

"In Britain, for example, people now say the differences between the two main political parties are very small. So, the risk we would see a dramatic change in economic policy with a change in government are greatly reduced," said Nikko's Thomson.
"Its much the same in the U.S. The policies (of the two main presidential candidates) are so similar that it's really more a a debate about personalities."

With bodies such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank seeking to impose a core policy of fiscal austerity and export-led growth on the world's developing nations, that critical mass will increase, analysts said.
But the drive to an all-embracing orthodoxy may turn out to be a double-edged sword.
While this conformity spreads to all corners of the globe, political risk may reappear in major industrialised nations, particularly in Europe.
"If you want to identify political risk in the next two to three years, it lies not in Russia, but in western Europe," said Thomson.
The only economic game being played in Europe is the push towards closer integration and a single currency. Any threat to that, would leave a dangerous vacuum, economists said.

"An awful lot in Europe hangs on this EMU (European Monetary Union) project. And there is no "plan B" in countries like France Italy, Spain, Belgium, even Germany...it is the dominant political issue for them," said DMG's Bell.
If EMU, set to start in 1999, goes ahead, all well and good.
But if it dissolves before starting, or collapses soon afterwards, the bricks and mortar of the most prominent, if not the only, support for economic policy in Europe would crumble.
"If EMU went, it would remove a consensus amongst European parties that reflects a great deal of political influence on economic policies," said Bell.

Furthermore, the drive to cut budget deficits and inflation to squeeze European economies into the shape required for a single currency has pushed countries such as Germany and France to the brink of, or even into, recession.
Unemployment has soared and popular support for a single currency has understandably waned.

Most of all, analysts warned against complacency, saying it would be dangerous for investors to treat the reduction of poltical risk asscociated with the old-style superpowers as a sign it has disappeared all together.
DMG's Bell said that with "market-friendly politicians in place across the world," political risk was not being taken as seriously as it it should.
"That will change," he said. "Unemployment is Europe's biggest problem, political mistrust of the centre is the United States' biggest problem and Japan has dramatic social change.
"At the moment all this is being suppressed. But people will get fed up. I see 1997 as quite a difficult year for the poltical world."
-- Kate Kelland, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 8682
